L9: # Register your interest in our dog cancer trial
L10: 
L11: We are recruiting dogs with mast cell cancer in Australia for an investigational trial of personalised mRNA cancer vaccines. Register your interest and share a few details about your dog. Our team will contact you about further screening.
L12: 
L13: 【5†Register your interest  →】 【8†See how it works  →】
L14: 
L15: Why we are running this trial
L16: ## From Rosie’s story to a future for more dogs.
L17: 
L18: 【9†Image: Rosie】
L19: 
L20: Rosie
L21: 
L22: The first dog treated with a personalised neoantigen vaccine.
L23: 
L24: It began with Rosie. Her experience with a personalised neoantigen vaccine encouraged Paul to explore how this approach could one day be made available to every dog with cancer.
L25: Before an approach like this can become broadly available, we must study it carefully and support it by evidence for review by the relevant veterinary regulators. This clinical trial is an important step in that process, helping us learn from participating dogs and understand the vaccine more fully.
L26: 
L27: 【2†Read Rosie’s personalised mRNA cancer-vaccine story  →】
L28: 
L29: Who can register
L30: ## If your dog has cancer and is currently in Australia, you’re welcome to register your interest. Our team will check whether your dog may be eligible for this trial.
L31: 
L32: 【5†Register your interest  →】
L33: 
L34: About the trial
L35: 
L36: ## What this trial is looking at
L37: 
L38: The trial will investigate a personalised mRNA vaccine approach for dogs with mast cell cancer. Tell us about your dog and our team will help determine whether they may be eligible for screening.
L39: 
L40: 【10†Image】
L41: ### Who can register
L42: 
L43: Dogs diagnosed with mast cell cancer who are based in, or able to travel within, Australia.
L44: 
L45: Every case is reviewed individually
L46: 
L47: 【11†Image】
L48: 
L49: ### The trial approach
L50: 
L51: A therapeutic mRNA vaccine designed from each dog’s own tumour and blood samples, intended to work alongside—not replace—existing care.
L52: 
L53: Personalised to each dog
L54: 
L55: 【12†Image】
L56: ### What screening involves
L57: 
L58: We help coordinate records, screening, sample logistics and updates, working with the trial team and your treating veterinarian.
L59: 
L60: A named team stays in touch
L61: 
L62: Trial registration and screening
L63: 
L64: ## How to register your interest.
L65: 
L66: You don’t need to have every record ready before registering your interest. Start with what you know and we’ll help with the rest.
L67: 
L68: 01
L69: ### Register your interest
L70: 
L71: Complete a short form with basic details about your dog, their mast cell cancer diagnosis and where you live.
L72: 
L73: 02
L74: 
L75: ### We get in touch
L76: 
L77: A Gamgee coordinator will contact you, answer practical questions and—with your permission—help gather relevant records from your vet.
L78: 
L79: 03
L80: ### The trial team confirms eligibility
L81: 
L82: The authorised study team and treating veterinarian assess potential eligibility. If your dog may proceed, you’ll receive the approved trial information and consent discussion before deciding.
L83: 
L84: These are indicative timings from a single case. Sequencing turnaround and manufacturing schedules may vary. We will give you a case-specific estimate before proceeding.
L85: 
L86: 【13†Image: A dog looking up at the camera】
L87: ## Ready to tell us about your dog?
L88: 
L89: Registering your interest does not guarantee eligibility or enrolment. Please continue your dog's existing veterinary care while your information is reviewed.
L90: 
L91: 【5†Register your interest  →】
L92:

L95: ## Stay informed
L96: 
L97: Get occasional updates on our research, clinical trials and progress in personalised cancer care for dogs.

L77: # Clinical Research
L78: 
L79: Much like clinical research in human medicine, veterinary clinical research is an essential part of improving future patient care and outcomes.
L80: 
L81: 【62†North Ryde】
L82: ## Why does SASH do clinical research?
L83: 
L84: SASH is committed to providing the best quality care to pets and their owners.
L85: 
L86: Much like clinical research in human medicine, veterinary clinical research is an essential part of improving future patient care and outcomes. Many of the methods and treatments used at SASH, and other veterinary hospitals, have come from various forms of veterinary research.
L87: Although SASH practices today’s best available veterinary medicine, using the latest equipment, it is also expected that further improvements can be made through continuous research. Through research, we are able to identify the best tests and treatments for our much loved pets.
L88: SASH is the largest veterinary specialist hospital in Australia. We have the combined expertise of around 50 veterinary specialists including neurology, imaging, anaesthesia, critical care and rehabilitation, which are rarely found elsewhere.
L89: 
L90: With SASH’s dedication to high quality patient care and seeking out industry leading veterinarians and scientists from across the world, SASH is at the forefront of veterinary care. In turn, this attracts thousands of cases per month.
L91: With the combination of the expertise of the SASH team and the high number of patients see, SASH is in a unique position to carry out no harm research. We aim to contribute to improving the care veterinarians can provide for pets throughout Australia.
L92: ## Clinical research at SASH
L93: 
L94: SASH conducts no harm research which is undertaken following ethics approval. The inclusion of patients in studies is on a voluntary basis and done following consultation and with the approval of pet owners.
L95: 
L96: SASH’s primary duty is to pets and pet owners. As such, it is important to note that patient care is paramount and will always take precedence over research needs.
L97: SASH is accredited as a veterinary research establishment, and all prospective research is approved by an external ethics committee.
L98: 
L99: Our research is lead by 【63†Dr Joanna White】, who holds a PhD, a Masters of Veterinary Science majoring in Veterinary Epidemiology and is a registered Small Animal Internal Medicine Specialist.
L100: Joanna is experienced in research study design, has been published in a number of leading veterinary journals, is an examiner at Fellowship level for the Australasian College of Veterinary Scientists in both internal and feline medicine and is currently Australia’s representative on the International Renal Interest Society.
L101: Research at SASH is supported by global animal health companies, such as IDEXX and charities such as the 【64†Australian Companion Animal Health Foundation†acahf.org】 (ACAHF), part of the Australian Small 【65†Animal Veterinary Association†www.ava.com.au】 and the Australian College of Veterinary Science specialist’s training grants.
L102: ## Examples of SASH clinical research
L103: ### Medicine
L104:   * Improved use of antibiotics to treat urinary tract infections (cystitis) to guide clinical decision-making.
L105:   * Investigating the link between age and risk of dehydration in cats. This may help reduce health issues associated with older cats during hot Australian summers.
L106:   * Optimising the use of radioactive iodine to treat hyperthryoidism, a very common hormonal problem in cats. This research aims to improve long term outcomes.
L107:   * Determining the impact of general anaesthetic on kidney function of cats with chronic kidney disease.
L108:   * Identifying risk factors associated with kidney stones, to help prevent this serious and painful condition in pets.
L109: ### Surgery
L110: 
L111:   *  World first research investigating the impact Double Pelvic Osteotomy (DPO), a form of surgery, for the treatment for canine hip dysplasia.
L112: 
L113: ### Rehabilitation
L114: 
L115:   *  Using exercise tolerance testing as a predictor of quality of life and survival in cancer patients.
L116: 
L117: ### Ophthalmology
L118: 
L119:   *  The use of how advanced imaging such as MRI and CT can be used to differentiate between causes of orbital disease, a condition that affects the eye socket.
L120: ### Oncology
L121: 
L122:   * The use of a combination of two chemotherapy medications and its effects in treating aggressive mast cell tumours.

L22: Treatment of Metastic Osteosarcoma
L23: New clinical trials have commenced at five Veterinary Oncology Specialist Centres within Australia for the trial of a drug to inhibit the spread of bone cancer.  The drug Auranofin has been tested in a mouse model with  results showing a significant reduction in the spread of osteosarcoma to the lungs without any side effects. It is hoped that similar results in the reduction of metastasis will be found with dogs.
L24: Auranofin also has the potential for the prevention and treatment of osteosarcoma in humans as well as dogs. Human hospitals are also participating in this study and are listed on the information sheet.
L25: The drug Auranofin will be free but there will be costs that owners will need to pay for themselves.  These other costs include those for monitoring the osteosarcoma such as blood tests, xrays and any other testing that the oncologist recommends.  Details of the expected cost will be provided when you contact the centres participating in the trial.
L26: If you have a dog with osteosarcoma and would like your dog to be considered for this trial please contact the Veterinary Oncology Centres listed in the five states participating in this trial:

L29:
